body: I don't remember if there's an actual reason or if it's just cleaner this way. Is there a reason to avoid record structs?
It's much less verbose as a record. Is there a reason for avoiding records?

Do you think it's safe to change this behavior without risking a regression? If not, then we can make the trampoline return it (to avoid having to handle two different signatures in the future) but ignore it from `CSharpInstance::raise_event_signal` for now.
`DelegateInvokeMethod` is already `IMethodSymbol`. The suggestion would make it seem as if we're doing a type check, when we're just checking that it's not null.

This `unsafe` is needed for the syntax `&trampoline`. It's not really an unsafe operation, but that's how C# treated unsafe code up until now (like a syntax thing). This seems to be changing in the future, but it will also be an optional thing you enable in projects 😬

The problem is that the safe approach requires reflection-related overhead and allocations. The user can avoid that by allowing unsafe code in their project.

> I would argue for the `unsafe` path only, if it has better performance, or is less code to maintain etc.

I don't think it's right for us to enable unsafe blocks in user projects. That should be some intentional decision by them. I don't even know if NuGet.org policies allow it.
Oh, yes. This should be checking `ScriptMethods`, `ScriptProperties`, and `ScriptSignals`, individually before calling the trampolines getter for each of them.

Yes, I was going to suggest looking up both hash maps. I didn't think the performance cost would be too high, but I'll take your word for it. Looks good as is. If you want, you could add a comment to explain why we're also adding static methods to `method_trampolines`, in case someone else gets confused in the future.
If we changed the generated code, I assume that would break the source generator tests so we'd notice. But it's fine to leave it like this.
Sounds good. If the middle part is **always** an int, we could make the `secondPart` type be `int`. But I think it's fine to leave the TODO you added, and fix it in a follow-up.

I agree that `is IMethodSymbol` doesn't make it entirely clear that it's checking that it's not null, but I feel like it's still better than `is { }` which doesn't read like a null check either. We could change it to `is not null` or `!= null` at the cost of slightly more verbosity. But if you feel really strongly about this, I'm fine keeping the change too.

That's a good point. I was thinking the behavior change would be desired, because I feel like I've seen issues before about signal invocations failing silently instead of printing an error. But I don't want to increase the scope of the PR, so let's do what you said. We can change the trampoline return now and leave `CSharpInstance::raise_event_signal` unchanged for now.

Right now, the generator checks the user project to see if it allows unsafe blocks, and then generates different code based on that. Since it's possible to make the generator work without requiring users to allow unsafe blocks, I feel like it would be better to use the same generated code everywhere.

> The problem is that the safe approach requires reflection-related overhead and allocations.

I wonder how big the cost of this is. I would expect the safe approach to not make that big of a difference, as @NoctemCat mentioned.

Personally, I don't like how records bring a bunch of unnecessary baggage that is compiler-synthesized and hidden. I would prefer to avoid them unless we actually needed the functionality they bring, at which point I would still prefer a non-record type that implements that functionality explicitly so it's clear what it does.

In this case, it didn't seem like a record was needed because this type is never compared or printed, so it looks like a simple struct definition would have sufficed.
This was an IDE suggested change, as far as I remember. Rider seems to prefer this syntax. But I don't mind changing it to a classic null check. It's the cast style that I found confusing.

What worries me is someone removing the old modifiers from the check when an update happens, forgetting that they are important for backwards compatibility. It seems safer this way. But if you want I can remove them.

Btw, I edited my original comment as I didn't express myself well. I meant that performance cost was **not** the reason (IIRC). It was just about compatibility, as looking up two hash maps would have introduced a regression in the example code.
My memory is failing me, but I think my concern here was more about startup time than GC allocations. But I didn't compare on any big project, so I have no idea if my concern is justified.
No, on second thought, I think you are right that it's safer this way.

I would really like to see some numbers to justify maintaining two paths before approving, but the PR is already a big improvement and I don't want it to miss the 4.8 release. Do you think you could measure the impact to help make a decision?

I don't really know how to measure that, unless I had some really big project where such an issue would be easily noticeable. Since we're in a hurry, I'll just remove it for now.
That being said, I think eventually it would be worth having two paths, because in the new `unsafe` model this is not considered an `unsafe` operation. Users would still have to enable this new model by themselves (hence why we would still need two paths), as it could cause build errors so it has to be their decision. But it becomes easier for them to decide to enable it as it doesn't require actually allowing unsafe code.
